title: Indian Sports Stars Break Silence, Back Student Protesters Demanding Education Reforms
excerpt: From Yuvraj Singh and Sachin Tendulkar to Abhinav Bindra and Manu Bhaker, India's biggest sporting icons are publicly supporting the CJP-led student movement demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET paper leak scandal.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indian sports icons are publicly supporting student protests for education reforms.
  • Protests demand resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over NEET paper leak.
  • Athletes like Yuvraj Singh and Sachin Tendulkar emphasize the importance of education.
  • The movement has gained national attention, with protests spreading across cities.
  • Support from athletes adds pressure on the government to address education issues.
Athletes Unite for Education Reform
›Yuvraj Singh calls for dialogue over confrontation.
›Sachin Tendulkar emphasizes meritocracy in education.
›Abhinav Bindra frames education as a non-partisan issue.
›Manu Bhaker highlights students' rights and futures.
›Sahal Abdul Samad condemns police violence against protesters.

India's sports fraternity has broken its characteristic silence on political matters, with a growing list of marquee athletes publicly backing the student-led protests that have gripped New Delhi and spread to cities across the country.

The demonstrations, led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), centre on demands for Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation following a paper leak in the NEET-UG 2026 medical entrance examination. What began as a sit-in at Delhi's Jantar Mantar has escalated into a nationwide movement, punctuated by a 'Chalo Sansad' march on July 20 that was met with police batons and tear gas.

Cricketers Lead the Charge

Former all-rounder Yuvraj Singh, a hero of India's 2011 World Cup triumph, posted an appeal on Instagram calling for dialogue over confrontation.

"To every child, student, woman and man: you deserve the opportunity to learn in peace, grow with safety and chase your dreams. Your well-being is the foundation of a brighter India. Through dialogue we can find an amicable solution for the sake of India's future."

— Yuvraj Singh, via Instagram

Sachin Tendulkar weighed in with a longer post invoking his late father, a professor. "A society which prioritises outcomes over effort will seek shortcuts over meritocracy," Tendulkar wrote. "When students feel disappointed that their hard work hasn't been rewarded, it is understandable."

India's current ODI and Test captain Shubman Gill shared his support on X: "As a young Indian, I believe our generation deserves every opportunity to learn, dream and shape the future we all aspire to."

Former opener Shikhar Dhawan urged patience while standing with the students: "India has always moved forward and will continue to progress." Mohammad Kaif was more pointed, writing: "As a father it pains me to see students being roughed up by police for protesting over flaws in education. Kids getting beaten with lathis on the streets of Delhi should stop."

Olympians and Champions Add Their Voices

Abhinav Bindra, India's first individual Olympic gold medallist, posted on X on July 23, framing the issue as non-partisan: "I have never considered myself a political person. But I do believe that some issues belong to all of us, regardless of where we stand. Education is one of them."

Double Olympic medallist shooter Manu Bhaker, one of the first athletes to speak out, called the students' demands a matter of fundamental rights. "The students and children who lost their lives were meant to be the future of our country. Their dreams, their potential, and their futures should have been protected," she wrote on July 17.

"Students are the future. Listen before they stop speaking. Nations don't grow by silencing questions. They grow by answering them."

— Nikhat Zareen, World Boxing Champion

Mohun Bagan midfielder Sahal Abdul Samad condemned the use of force directly: "Nothing justifies lathis on a generation that brought nothing but its voice. Their voices deserve a seat at the table, not a barricade in front of it."

Timeline of the Student Protests
May 2026
Chief Justice's comments spark the CJP movement.
July 17, 2026
Manu Bhaker speaks out on students' rights.
July 20, 2026
Nationwide 'Chalo Sansad' march met with police force.
July 23, 2026
Abhinav Bindra posts support for education reform.

Why Athletes Speaking Up Matters

Indian sportspersons have historically avoided taking public positions on political controversies. The roster of names now backing the students — spanning cricket, shooting, boxing, and football — signals an unusual shift, particularly given the commercial risks of antagonising authorities.

The cricketers' wives have also been vocal. Suryakumar Yadav's wife Devisha Shetty criticised the violence during the Sansad Chalo march, while Rohit Sharma's wife Ritika Sajdeh shared a viral video of a nine-year-old protester declaring he was not afraid of police lathis.

The movement itself traces to May 2026, when comments by India's Chief Justice comparing youth to cockroaches sparked the satirical CJP movement, which has since evolved into a serious platform for demands around education accountability, employment, and student welfare. Tensions peaked after Delhi's Chhatrasal Stadium was converted into a temporary detention facility during the July 20 march, and environmental activist Sonam Wangchuk launched an indefinite hunger strike in solidarity.

![Yuvraj Singh. Athletes like Yuvraj Singh and Sachin Tendulkar emphasize the importance of education.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/81/Yuvraj_Singh_appointed_as_Ulysse_Nardin_watch_brand_ambassador.jpeg)

What Comes Next

With the Monsoon Session of Parliament now underway, the protesters' core demands — Pradhan's resignation, accountability for the NEET leak, and structural education reforms — are expected to dominate debate. The government has yet to formally respond to the athletes' appeals, though the broadening support base from India's most visible public figures adds pressure.

For the Indian diaspora, many of whom navigated the same competitive examination system, the movement has resonated across social media. Parents and former students abroad have organised solidarity vigils, recognising the systemic issues that shaped their own educational journeys.
